title: Finite-Wing CFD Analysis of a 2m UAV Wing in ANSYS Fluent
goal: Perform a baseline finite-wing CFD analysis for a 2 m wingspan UAV designed to carry a 5 kg payload for design decisions
context:
The problem I am solving is the preliminary aerodynamic evaluation of a small fixed-wing UAV with a 2 m wingspan and a 5 kg payload requirement. Before building or testing the complete aircraft, I need to establish whether the proposed wing can generate sufficient lift while maintaining reasonable aerodynamic efficiency. At this stage, the goal is not to produce a highly detailed aircraft design, but to create a reliable baseline aerodynamic model that can be used to understand the wing's behavior.
The main challenge is that the wing's aerodynamic performance depends on several interconnected design choices. The airfoil selection affects the lift and drag characteristics, while the wing's chord, aspect ratio, and operating conditions determine how the selected airfoil behaves as a finite wing. Once the geometry is established, the surrounding fluid domain, mesh resolution, turbulence model, and solver settings can also influence the CFD results. Therefore, I need to make these decisions in a logical sequence rather than choosing them independently.
I am solving this problem because the CFD analysis will provide an early indication of whether the wing configuration is aerodynamically suitable for the UAV's intended mission. The analysis will allow me to examine lift, drag, lift-to-drag ratio, pressure distribution, velocity distribution, and overall flow behavior without needing to physically manufacture and test the wing first. The results can also reveal areas that may need to be changed, such as the airfoil, wing geometry, or operating condition.

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: Yes, I achieved the goal within the approximately one-hour session. Claude helped me select a suitable airfoil for the 2 m wingspan, 5 kg payload UAV, establish the initial finite-wing configuration, and make decisions regarding the CFD domain, meshing strategy, solver setup, and convergence criteria. I was then able to implement these recommendations in ANSYS and complete the baseline finite-wing CFD analysis, obtaining the aerodynamic results needed to evaluate the wing's performance.

Step 1-2.step_action: Ask Claude to evaluate and recommend a suitable airfoil for a 2 m wingspan UAV designed to carry a 5 kg payload, comparing candidates on lift capability, aerodynamic efficiency, stall characteristics, and low-Reynolds-number suitability; then move directly into finite-wing configuration guidance before importing geometry.

nodes.label: State UAV requirements and request airfoil alternatives
nodes.detail: The participant opens a new Claude chat and describes a 2 m wingspan UAV carrying up to 5 kg payload, noting they already have NACA 0012 in mind and asking Claude to suggest other candidate airfoils before starting the CFD workflow.

nodes.label: Compare candidate airfoils and recommend a baseline/comparison set
nodes.detail: Claude returns a comparison table (Clark Y, Eppler E205/E212, SD7062/SD7037, NACA 4412/2412, MH-series) discussing Reynolds-number sensitivity, max Cl, L/D, and manufacturability, then recommends running NACA 0012 as the documented baseline case while comparing Clark Y and SD7062 as cambered candidates. It asks the participant for chord length, cruise speed, and whether the study is 2D or full 3D.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about comparing and recommending candidate airfoils
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's comparison of airfoil alternatives (e.g., Clark Y and other cambered sections versus the symmetric NACA 0012) and its suggested baseline/comparison set.

nodes.label: Confirm NACA 0012 and announce geometry import
nodes.detail: The participant decides to proceed with NACA 0012 and tells Claude they will start their analysis by importing the wing geometry they already created in Fusion 360.

nodes.label: Give pre-import domain and meshing guidance
nodes.detail: Before the participant imports the geometry, Claude proactively lays out what to nail down first: export format (.step/.iges) for clean DesignModeler import, whether the study is a 2D section or full 3D wing, and domain/meshing considerations to expect right after import -- enclosure/farfield sizing of roughly 10-15x chord length, boundary-layer inflation near the airfoil surface, and named selections for inlet/outlet/wall/farfield. This guidance is applied later during the actual meshing phase without being re-asked in the same form.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about pre-import domain and meshing guidance
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's pre-import checklist (export format, 2D vs 3D, bare wing vs full aircraft, enclosure sizing and meshing considerations) before moving to the geometry work.

Step 3.step_name: Create the wing geometry and the computational domain
Step 3.step_action: Use the selected airfoil configuration to create the 3D finite wing in ANSYS: export the existing Fusion 360 geometry, import into DesignModeler, build an enclosure as the external flow domain, Boolean-subtract the wing to carve a cavity, and cut the domain in half along the symmetry plane. Before entering the meshing app, ask Claude for a mesh strategy.

nodes.label: Review and export the existing wing geometry from Fusion 360
nodes.detail: The participant opens Autodesk Fusion 360 to the 'FAN DESIGN CFD' project and the already-modeled 'NACA 0012 Airfoil Wing' part -- a NACA0012 airfoil with 1 m chord and 1 m span, symmetric about its own plane -- and exports it as a STEP file for universal CAD compatibility.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: 1a ask the suggestion other than naca 0012, and export naca 0012 on 2a

nodes.label: Import geometry into ANSYS DesignModeler
nodes.detail: The participant switches to ANSYS Workbench, drags in a Fluid Flow (Fluent) system, and imports the STEP geometry into DesignModeler, where the wing appears as a small lofted solid body.

nodes.label: Create the enclosure as the external fluid domain
nodes.detail: An Enclosure (Box shape, non-uniform cushion values, ~4 m/2 m/2 m clearance with larger clearance on the outlet side to let the wake develop) is created around the wing to act as the CFD domain boundary.

nodes.label: Describe their plan to use Boolean subtraction approach
nodes.detail: Having built the enclosure, the participant asks Claude whether Boolean-subtracting the wing from the enclosure body is the best way to obtain the fluid domain.

nodes.label: Confirm Boolean-subtraction approach for carving the wing cavity
nodes.detail: The participant describes their plan to use Boolean subtraction after creating the enclosure, and Claude confirms this is the standard, correct approach for carving the wing shape out of the enclosure to form the fluid cavity, clarifying target vs. tool body selection.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about confirming the Boolean-subtraction approach
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's confirmation that Boolean subtraction (target = enclosure, tool = wing, preserve tool bodies = No) is the standard way to carve out the fluid domain, along with its cautions.

nodes.label: Clarify they are simulating a 3D wing rather than a 2D section
nodes.detail: The participant clarifies to Claude that the simulation is for a 3D wing rather than a 2D airfoil section.

nodes.label: Adjust domain guidance for a full 3D wing
nodes.detail: The participant clarifies they are simulating a 3D wing rather than a 2D section, and Claude updates its guidance on enclosure and domain sizing to account for wingtip effects and 3D wake development rather than a simple 2D airfoil domain.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about adjusting domain guidance for a full 3D wing
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's 3D-wing domain guidance: enclosure shape options and sizing relative to chord (about 10-15c upstream, 20-25c downstream, 5-10c beyond the tip).

nodes.label: Tell Claude they plan to use the symmetry option to save computation time
nodes.detail: After reading Claude's half-span vs full-span section, the participant replies in the chat that they plan to use the symmetry option to save computation time.

nodes.label: Confirm symmetry-plane cut is the right move
nodes.detail: Claude confirms that using the ZX symmetry plane as a cutting tool is the correct approach for a wing-alone case and outlines what to set up (symmetry boundary condition, half-domain enclosure).

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about confirming the symmetry-plane cut approach
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's confirmation that a half-wing with a symmetry plane is the right move, including how the enclosure should sit flush at the symmetry plane and which named selections to create.

nodes.label: Boolean-subtract the wing from the enclosure and cut the domain along the symmetry plane
nodes.detail: In DesignModeler the participant adds a Boolean operation with the enclosure as target and the wing as tool, sets the operation to Subtract with Preserve Tool Bodies = No, and generates the fluid domain. Explaining that the airfoil and the whole setup are symmetric, they then apply a Symmetry feature on the ZX plane to keep only one half of the domain, halving the cell count, while keeping the enclosure size they set earlier.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: adopt the boolean subtraction in designmodeler

nodes.label: Return to Workbench and open ANSYS Meshing
nodes.detail: The participant returns to the Workbench project and launches ANSYS Meshing, waiting for the geometry to load.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for a basic mesh strategy before starting meshing
nodes.detail: With the geometry/domain complete, the participant asks Claude for a basic mesh strategy that produces a clean mesh without an excessive cell count, in preparation for switching to ANSYS Meshing.

nodes.label: Provide a lean meshing strategy
nodes.detail: Claude recommends a hybrid tetrahedral/polyhedral bulk mesh with prism inflation layers on the wing surface, a first-layer y+ target of ~1 (or ~30-50 with wall functions), 15-20 inflation layers with a 1.15-1.2 growth rate, and local body/face-sizing refinement zones at the wingtip vortex and wake region rather than uniformly refining the whole domain.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about a lean meshing strategy
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's lean meshing strategy: a hybrid mesh with prism inflation layers on the wing, first-layer height from target y+, and local refinement for the tip vortex and wake.

Step 4.step_action: Implement the meshing strategy in ANSYS Meshing: generate and refine the surface mesh, add wake and named-selection controls, and set up boundary-layer inflation, asking Claude one targeted follow-up question about inflation geometry/boundary selection along the way.

nodes.label: Generate the default coarse mesh and identify under-resolved regions
nodes.detail: The participant generates ANSYS's default mesh (element size ~5e-2 m, CFD physics preference, Fluent solver preference) and observes that the region around the airfoil surface is not well resolved by the coarse triangulation.

nodes.label: Add and refine Face Sizing on the wing surface
nodes.detail: Following the earlier mesh-strategy guidance, the participant adds a Face Sizing control on the wing surface and progressively refines the element size from the ~5e-2 m default down toward ~4.5e-3 m and then 5e-3 m, producing visibly finer triangulation concentrated around the leading and trailing edges.

nodes.label: Add Body Sizing to refine the wake region
nodes.detail: A Body Sizing control is added behind the wing to refine the wake region, matching the wake-refinement-zone advice from the earlier mesh-strategy answer.

nodes.label: Create Named Selections for Fluent domain regions
nodes.detail: The participant creates Named Selections so Fluent will recognize the domain regions: 'symmetry' for the ZX cutting plane, 'inlet' for the velocity-inlet face, 'outlet' for the pressure-outlet face, 'walls' for the remaining enclosure faces, and 'wing' for the airfoil surface itself (more fiddly since the wing is embedded inside the enclosure cavity, requiring box-select after switching mesh display mode).

nodes.label: Ask Claude specifically what geometry and boundary to select for it
nodes.detail: While setting up inflation in ANSYS Meshing, the participant asks Claude what to select for the geometry and boundary fields of the inflation control.

nodes.label: Answer a targeted follow-up on inflation geometry and boundary selection
nodes.detail: Before adding the boundary-layer inflation control, the participant asks Claude specifically what geometry and boundary to select for it. Claude explains the Inflation Option choices in ANSYS Meshing (Smooth Transition as the easiest default vs. Total Thickness vs. First Layer Thickness for direct y+-derived control), recommends applying inflation only to the 'wing' named selection (not farfield or symmetry), and repeats the growth-rate (1.15-1.2) and layer-count (15-20) settings, flagging the wingtip and leading-edge regions as common spots for inflation-layer collapse. This is a genuine new, targeted exchange distinct from the earlier general mesh-strategy answer, not merely re-read prior guidance.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about inflation geometry and boundary selection
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's answer: select the fluid-domain body as geometry and the wing-surface named selection as boundary, and do not apply inflation on the symmetry plane or far-field faces.

nodes.label: Add 15 inflation layers on the wing surface
nodes.detail: Applying Claude's answer, the participant adds an Inflation control on the 'wing' named selection with 15 layers hugging the wing surface, checking that the near-wing region resolves into fine prism layers for the boundary layer.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: use the same inflation setting suggested by claude

nodes.label: Finalize the mesh and complete the meshing phase
nodes.detail: A second Face Sizing pass is added, the mesh (Face Sizing, Body Sizing, second Face Sizing, Inflation) is regenerated and checked for adequacy, and the participant declares meshing complete before moving into Fluent solver setup.

Step 5.step_name: Set up the Fluent simulation, run, monitor, and interpret results
Step 5.step_action: Run the finite-wing simulation in ANSYS Fluent while monitoring residuals and aerodynamic force coefficients, confirming the turbulence-model and boundary-condition plan with Claude, then switch to CFD-Post to build contours and troubleshoot apparent anomalies with Claude before reviewing the final force data.

nodes.label: Launch the Fluent solver
nodes.detail: The participant launches the Fluent solver from ANSYS Workbench with a 3D, double-precision setup and parallel processing (2 solver processes).

nodes.label: Ask Claude to confirm the steady-state analysis and turbulence-model plan
nodes.detail: Before configuring physics in Fluent, the participant describes their plan to perform a steady-state analysis and asks Claude to weigh in on the turbulence model choice for the UAV wing.

nodes.label: Recommend k-omega SST with a Transition SST trade-off note
nodes.detail: Claude confirms k-omega SST is a solid baseline choice for the low-Re UAV wing, but flags Transition SST (gamma-Re-theta) as a more accurate alternative that captures laminar separation bubbles and gives better Cl/Cd prediction near stall, at the cost of needing a finer y+~1 mesh. It suggests a first pass with plain k-omega SST and wall functions (y+~30-50) for a fast baseline, then refining later.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about turbulence model recommendations and trade-offs
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's confirmation that k-omega SST suits the 30 m/s steady external-aero case, with its note to check the Reynolds number and the Transition SST trade-off.

nodes.label: Describe the planned boundary-condition setup to Claude
nodes.detail: The participant tells Claude they plan to set up the simulation with a velocity inlet at 30 m/s and a pressure outlet, asking for a review before proceeding.

nodes.label: Confirm the BC workflow and give refinements
nodes.detail: Claude confirms the velocity-inlet/pressure-outlet plus hybrid-initialization workflow is correct and recommends refinements before hitting Calculate: set a low inlet turbulence intensity (~0.5-1%) and viscosity ratio (~5-10) instead of Fluent's default 5%, apply the same low turbulence at the outlet for backflow, confirm the symmetry plane is typed as Symmetry (not Wall), tighten the residual criteria to 1e-6 rather than the default 1e-3, monitor Cl/Cd via lift/drag report definitions, use the Coupled scheme with second-order upwind discretization, run 2000-5000 iterations, and check the Reference Values (half-wing planform area, root chord, 30 m/s).

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about the boundary condition workflow and refinements
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's refinements to the boundary-condition plan: lower the inlet/outlet turbulence intensity from Fluent's default 5% to ~0.5-1%, verify the symmetry boundary type, use 1e-6 residuals instead of the default 1e-3, monitor Cl/Cd directly, use Coupled with second-order upwind, run many more iterations, and check the reference values.

nodes.label: Configure solver physics in Fluent
nodes.detail: The participant sets up pressure-based, steady-state physics with the k-omega SST viscous model (SST k-omega options, Production Limiter enabled) and sets air as the working fluid.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: follow claude suggestion on using k omega sst in fluent

nodes.label: Set up boundary conditions and discretization
nodes.detail: The inlet is configured as a velocity-inlet at 30 m/s, keeping Fluent's default turbulence specification (5% intensity, viscosity ratio 10) rather than the low intensity Claude suggested; the outlet is confirmed as a pressure-outlet (backflow turbulence also left at the default 5%/10), the symmetry and wall boundary conditions are verified, and the solution methods are set to the Coupled scheme with second-order upwind spatial discretization.

nodes.label: Set convergence criteria and create force reports
nodes.detail: Residual convergence criteria are set to 1e-3 (Fluent's default, judged adequate for a baseline run), and two force report definitions are created to monitor aerodynamic coefficients during the run: a drag report (checking the force-vector direction lies along the flow's x-axis) and a lift report.

nodes.label: Initialize and run the solver
nodes.detail: After hybrid initialization, the participant sets up 300 iterations and starts the calculation, watching the Scaled Residuals plot (continuity, x/y/z-velocity, k, omega) drop over the first several dozen iterations.

user_response.label: modify
user_response.reasoning: adopt the ci/cd monitor with modification

nodes.label: Monitor convergence to completion
nodes.detail: The solve is monitored over an extended period; the participant periodically checks progress (noting ~76 iterations complete at one point), and the solution reaches the 1e-3 convergence criterion, reporting 'Calculation complete' around the 84th-85th iteration, well short of the full 300 iterations budgeted.

nodes.label: Switch to CFD-Post and build a pressure contour
nodes.detail: With the solver finished, the participant closes it and opens ANSYS CFD-Post, inserts a plane, and builds a pressure contour on the wing surface, observing values ranging from about -806 Pa to 566 Pa across the surface.

nodes.label: Build a velocity contour and interpret the physics
nodes.detail: A velocity-magnitude contour is built on the wing surface and symmetry plane. The participant identifies the leading-edge stagnation region (high pressure, near-zero velocity, shown in red) as physically correct, observes the top/bottom surface pressure difference that generates lift, and examines flow separation and a turbulent wake forming behind the wing.

nodes.label: Flag apparent 'dead spot' anomalies to Claude
nodes.detail: The participant notices two suspicious dead-spot-looking regions above and below the wing in the contour and shares a screenshot with Claude, asking for its thoughts.

nodes.label: Flag the red/yellow patches as likely mesh artifacts
nodes.detail: Claude points out that while the red leading-edge blob is near the expected stagnation point, its distinct circular shape (rather than a smooth stagnation gradient) looks more like a mesh artifact or poorly resolved region, and the isolated yellow trailing patch looks detached from the wake rather than smooth wake physics. It asks about the min velocity value and the angle of attack.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about flagging mesh artifacts in the results
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's assessment that the red spot at the leading edge is likely the stagnation point and that the circular patches may be mesh or plotting artifacts worth checking.

nodes.label: Clarify the angle of attack is 0 degrees
nodes.detail: The participant confirms the simulation is run at AoA = 0 degrees.

nodes.label: Explain why AoA=0 makes the result more suspicious and give a checklist
nodes.detail: Claude explains that at AoA=0 with a symmetric NACA 0012 airfoil, the flow field should be clean and symmetric with no reason for large velocity reversal away from the stagnation point, making the distinct circular red/yellow patches more likely a mesh or setup issue. It gives an ordered checklist: inspect the mesh at that exact region in ANSYS Meshing for bad-quality cells, inflation-layer collapse, or gaps/non-manifold geometry left from the Boolean subtract.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about diagnosing suspicious AoA=0 results
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's explanation that at 0 degrees AoA on a symmetric NACA 0012 the field should be nearly symmetric, so the patches look more suspicious, and its checklist for diagnosing them.

nodes.label: Point out the flow is not actually 0 m/s there
nodes.detail: The participant pushes back, noting that the flow in that region is not actually 0 m/s, prompting Claude to reconsider its assessment.

nodes.label: Clarify that the plotted variable is a velocity component, not magnitude
nodes.detail: Claude re-examines the zoomed contour and clarifies this is not a mesh defect: the plotted 'Velocity u' variable is the X-component of velocity only, not the total velocity magnitude, so near-zero or negative values there simply mean the flow is redirected around the airfoil, not that the flow has actually stopped.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about clarifying the plotted variable in the velocity field
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's clarification that the plotted variable is 'Velocity u' (the X-component), so near-zero or negative values do not mean the flow speed is zero there.

nodes.label: Switch the contour to velocity magnitude in CFD-Post and share it with Claude
nodes.detail: Following Claude's explanation that 'Velocity u' is only the X-component, the participant returns to CFD-Post, changes the contour variable from 'Velocity u' to 'Velocity' (magnitude), regenerates the plot, and shares a screenshot of the entire velocity-magnitude contour with Claude to settle the question.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: set the cfd post by adopting claude suggestion

nodes.label: Confirm the velocity field is clean and physically correct
nodes.detail: Claude confirms the velocity magnitude plot is clean and physical: the red leading-edge patch is the true stagnation point (min value ~0 m/s), the thin green/teal band hugging the wing is the boundary layer recovering smoothly, the yellow-green trailing patch is the upper/lower boundary layers merging into the wake, and the uniform ~30-34 m/s freestream matches the 30 m/s inlet condition -- concluding there is no dead spot or mesh defect.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about confirming the velocity field is physically correct
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's confirmation that the full velocity-magnitude plot is clean and physical: stagnation at the leading edge, a thin boundary layer, and accelerated flow over the surfaces.

nodes.label: Review the Report File Definitions and Forces panel
nodes.detail: The participant scrolls back through the Report File Definitions dialog and the Forces panel in Fluent, reviewing the drag (report-def-0) and lift (report-def-1) report definitions and their pressure/viscous/total coefficient breakdowns on the wing zone as a final check of the extracted force data.

nodes.label: Ask Claude to generate a Cl/Cd signature plot
nodes.detail: The participant tells Claude the Cl and Cd plot resembles a typical result for a symmetric airfoil and asks it to generate an image illustrating that expected signature.

nodes.label: Generate and explain the symmetric-airfoil Cl/Cd signature
nodes.detail: Claude generates an illustrative image and explains that this is the expected signature for a symmetric airfoil at 0 degrees AoA: Cl settles near zero and Cd settles to a small, steady value once the residuals converge, matching what the participant observed in their own run.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about the symmetric-airfoil Cl/Cd signature
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's explanation that Cl settling near zero and Cd converging to a small positive value is the expected signature for a symmetric airfoil at 0 degrees AoA, along with its suggestion to run an AoA sweep next.
